fits each of them, and whether a member of an overload is one that Viewpoint does not let an addon change. The consent
dialog is then already past. The card says **Failed**,
with the reason, and the game does not change.

If Viewpoint refuses a hook, the card shows the hook, the refusal and the reason. The addon stays **Inactive** until you
correct the jar.

Viewpoint can also refuse hooks on a game class that cannot take hooks together with Viewpoint's own changes. The card
then names the class.

## Good and bad targets

| Good | Bad |
| --- | --- |
| A method that the game calls one time each tick or less: an update, an event, a click. | A method that the game calls thousands of times each frame, for example a square accessor. It is a **costly hook**, unless the handler is [typed](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/patching/managed-patching.md#typed-handlers). |
| A method with one clear overload, selected by its descriptor. | A method whose result depends on a different thread. |
| A hook that only reads. | A hook that skips a method that the game needs. |

## Threads

The game calls some methods from threads that are not the main thread. Viewpoint does not run a `thread = MAIN`
handler for those calls, and counts them. A method of Viewpoint that runs on the render thread takes only a
`thread = RENDER` hook. Viewpoint refuses a `MAIN` hook on it. See
[Managed patching](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/patching/managed-patching.md#threads).

> **Caution**
>
> A new game build can change the target methods. Set `game.min` and `game.max` to the builds that you tested. If a target
> method is not in a new build, the hook does not install, and the card tells you.

---

# Permissions

> The permissions that an addon can ask for, what each one opens, and what occurs without it.

Put the services that your addon uses in `permissions`. The player reads this list before they give consent. Viewpoint
refuses a call that is not in the list.

```properties
permissions=hooks,files,downloads
hooks.targets=zombie.characters.IsoPlayer
files.quotaMiB=16
downloads.hosts=github.com,objects.githubusercontent.com
```

| Permission | Opens | Keys | Page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `hooks` | `@Hook` handlers, and `@Patch` classes in an addon jar. Game methods and listed methods of Viewpoint. | `hooks.targets` | [Managed patching](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/patching/managed-patching.md) |
| `files` | `AddonFiles`: a folder for your addon, with a quota | `files.quotaMiB` (optional) | [Files](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/files.md) |
| `downloads` | `AddonDownloads`: a download that the player accepts each time | `downloads.hosts` | [Downloads](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/downloads.md) |
| `lua` | `@LuaExport`: Java functions that the Lua of any mod can call | `lua.globals` (optional) | [Lua exports](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/lua-exports.md) |
| `camera` | Camera layers, camera claims, look control, view control and cursor claims | None | [Camera layers](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/camera-layers.md) |
| `combat` | Aim and shot listeners, sway, shot resolvers and reticles | None | [Aim & shots](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/aim-and-shots.md) |
| `models` | `ModelProvider` and `AttachmentProvider` | None | [Model providers](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/model-providers.md) |
| `shaders` | `ShaderValues` and `AddonSnippets` | None | [Shader values](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/shader-values.md), [Shader snippets](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/shader-snippets.md) |
| `draw` | `DrawCallback` and the `Gpu` object | `draw.gpuMiB` (optional) | [Draw callbacks](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/draw-callbacks.md) |
| `vram` | More than 128 MiB of video memory for the `Gpu` objects | `draw.gpuMiB` | [Draw callbacks](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/draw-callbacks.md) |

These need **no** permission:

- the view state;
- your settings, your settings page and your keys;
- your own assets;
- services (`Services`). A new `exports=` package needs the player's consent.

## Without the permission

| Use | Without the permission |
| --- | --- |
| `AddonFiles` | Each call gives a `SecurityException`. |
| `AddonDownloads` | Each call gives a `SecurityException`. |
| A registration through the context, for example a camera layer, a provider or a draw callback | The call gives a `SecurityException`. |
| `@Hook` | Viewpoint refuses the jar when it reads it. |
| A hook on a class that is not in `hooks.targets` | Viewpoint refuses the jar when it reads it. |
| `@LuaExport` | Viewpoint refuses the jar when it reads it. |

## Permissions and labels

A permission is not a label. The permissions list what the addon **asks for**. The label tells what the **code** uses.
The card shows both, on the **Trust** and **Permissions** tabs.

- A hook can keep the label Normal. Its target must be a game method that Viewpoint has reviewed. It must use
  `thread = MAIN` and a fast handler.
- A `thread = ANY` hook makes the label Amber.
- A `draw` permission makes the label Amber: the addon draws with OpenGL.
- `java.nio.file` makes the label Red, also with the `files` permission. Use `AddonFiles`.

## When you change the permissions

These changes need the player's consent again:

- a new permission;
- a new class in `hooks.targets`;
- a new hooked member of Viewpoint;
- a new host in `downloads.hosts`;
- a larger `files.quotaMiB`;
- a new Lua export or Lua global;
- a new snippet point or draw point;
- a new kind of claim (camera, view, shot resolver, reticle or cursor);
- a new `exports=` package, or a new `requires`;
- a new member of Viewpoint that you use, reflect or hook.

Until the player gives consent, the addon stays off. This is also true if it was active before. See
[Updates & changelogs](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/trust/updates-and-changelogs.md).

> **Tip**
>
> Ask only for what you need. Each permission is more text for the player to read. Each new item is one more consent
> dialog.

---

# Labels

> What makes a label Normal, Amber or Red, the extra lines of a card, and the texts that the player sees.

Each managed package has a label on its card. Viewpoint's automatic check sets the label when it loads the package. The
label tells what the check found in this version of the package. It is not a statement about the author.

## The three levels

| Level | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Normal** | The code uses only `viewpoint.api` and the parts of Java and the game that Viewpoint accepts. The card shows no badge. |
| **Amber** | The code uses something that the player must look at. The card gives the reasons. |
| **Red** | The code can do things outside Viewpoint's control. The card gives the reasons. The addon stays off until the player allows it, with a second confirmation. |

One Red reason makes the label Red. One Amber reason, and no Red reason, makes the label Amber.

## Get a Normal label

- Use `viewpoint.api` and plain Java: maths, strings, collections, time.
- Use `AddonFiles` for files.
- Use `AddonDownloads` for downloads.
- Use `AddonAssets` for models, textures, sounds and data.
- Use services, camera layers, aim and shot listeners, providers and shader values for what they cover.
- Do your work on the main thread.
- Hook game methods with `thread = MAIN`, and keep the handlers fast.
- Extend only Java classes or `viewpoint.api` types, not game classes.

An addon that uses or hooks a member of Viewpoint from the internals list is never Normal.

## What makes a label Amber

The addon:

- starts background threads;
- sends multiplayer messages;
- calls Lua;
- uses parts of Java or the game that Viewpoint has not reviewed;
- extends a class that Viewpoint has not reviewed;
- has a hook with `thread = ANY`;
- has a **costly hook**: a hook on a method that the game calls very frequently;
- has a **slow hook**: a handler that takes too much time;
- **draws with OpenGL**: it has a draw callback, and it uses the `Gpu` object or the short list of OpenGL calls that
  Viewpoint allows;
- uses or hooks a member of Viewpoint that has the Amber grade in the
  [Viewpoint internals list](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/reference/viewpoint-internals.md);
- uses a deprecated member of Viewpoint.

## What makes a label Red

The addon:

- reads or writes files outside its folder;
- opens network connections;
- uses reflection;
- starts programs;
- loads native code;
- defines classes;
- uses LWJGL beyond the allowed OpenGL calls: it can read and write any memory of the game;
- uses OpenGL directly, outside the draw callbacks and the allowed calls;
- stops the game process, or changes settings of the full Java process;
- uses game code that reads files or opens network connections;
- has a hook with `thread = RENDER`;
- uses or hooks a member of Viewpoint that has the Red grade in the
  [Viewpoint internals list](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/reference/viewpoint-internals.md);
- links to the code of an addon that is Red. The reason reads **uses code of X (Red)**.

An addon that links to the code of another addon (with `requires` and `exports`) takes the highest level of the addons it
links to. See [Services](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/services.md).

## What Viewpoint does not load

Viewpoint does not load a jar that breaks one of these rules. The card names the cause.

- Do not use ZombieBuddy or ByteBuddy. The one exception is the `@Patch` and `@Exposer.LuaClass` annotations, which
  Viewpoint reads and removes. See [Migrating from ZombieBuddy](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/patching/migrating-from-zombiebuddy.md).
- Use only the members on the [Viewpoint internals list](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/reference/viewpoint-internals.md), and only in the way that the
  list allows.
- Do not use a member that Viewpoint has removed (the card shows **Needs an update**).
- Do not make class loaders, and do not define classes.
- Do not declare native methods, and do not load native code (`System.load`, `System.loadLibrary`, `java.lang.foreign`).
- Do not use LWJGL calls that reach memory by its address: everything in `org.lwjgl.system` (`MemoryUtil`,
  `MemoryStack`, `Callback`, `Struct`), `PointerBuffer`, the `n`-prefixed functions, a `long` that is a pointer (for
  example in `glReadPixels`, `glDrawElements` and `glVertexAttribPointer`), and the calls that load a library. A `long`
  that is a size or an offset (`glBufferData`) is allowed. Other LWJGL calls are allowed but make the card Red.
- Do not put a class of the game, Java or a library in your jar under its own name.
- Do not ask for an agent or more access in the jar's manifest (`Class-Path`, `Launcher-Agent-Class`, `Add-Opens` and the like).
- Do not use a multi-release jar or a `module-info`.
- Do not put your classes in a package of Viewpoint, the game, ZombieBuddy or ByteBuddy.
- Do not write to a field of Viewpoint. Use the API that replaces the write, for example camera layers.

If the jar is too large or too complex for the check, the card shows **Cannot be checked**. The addon stays off. Make the
jar smaller and simpler.

## Resource packs and Shaderpacks

A resource pack has no Java. Viewpoint reads its files with its own loaders. If a file is not correct, the card tells
you which one.

A Shaderpack has no Java also. Its label says that it is graphics code only, and it shows the licence. Viewpoint checks
the size and the form of the code. It does not check what the code computes.

## The extra lines of a card

Some cards have a line below the label. These lines do not change the level.

**The Lua line.** Each label has a last line about Lua. Viewpoint does not check Lua.

- **Has Lua: not checked by Viewpoint**, then the names of some functions that Viewpoint found in the Lua. Examples are
  `getModFileWriter`, `getHostByName`, or use of the clipboard. The names are in the text "Found in it:";
- or **No Lua**.

**The export line.** An addon that gives Java functions to Lua adds a text to the Lua line. The text says that any mod's
Lua can call N functions of its Java. The card lists what they use. An export does not raise the level. If one of the functions can reach
something that is Red, the reason reads "…, callable from any mod's Lua". The text counts the functions that the exports
call. It does not count code that runs when a class loads, or an object that the addon stored for later.

**The shader line.** A card of a Shaderpack, and of an addon with shader snippets or `Gpu` programs, has the shader line.
See the texts below.

**Draws over the whole screen.** The card of an addon that draws at the `final` point or the `crosshair` point says this.
A drawing at the `final` point can cover the whole screen. A drawing there can hide the game.

## The texts that the player sees

**Normal** has no badge. Its tooltip is:

> Checked by Viewpoint. This addon's Java code uses only parts of Java, the game and Viewpoint that Viewpoint has reviewed. Viewpoint found no way for it to reach your files outside its own folder, the internet, other programs or native code. It can still change anything in your game and saves. In multiplayer, what it puts into the game is sent to the server. The mod's Lua scripts are not checked. Its assets are checked for their form and size, not for what they do.

**Amber**:

> Uses things Viewpoint has not reviewed: \{background threads · multiplayer messages · Lua · draws with OpenGL · internals of Viewpoint · hooks that run on any thread · other parts of Java and the game · code of other addons\}. Viewpoint cannot tell what these lead to. Turn it on only if you trust the author.

**Red**, off until the player allows it:

> Can \{read and write your files · reach the internet · start programs · load native code · change the game's code · reach any part of the game by name · stop the game or change settings of the whole game · read and write any memory of the game · use OpenGL outside the draw callbacks · use internals of Viewpoint that are graded Red · hook the render thread · do what the addons it links to can do\}. Viewpoint cannot protect you from what this addon does. Allow it only for authors you trust.

In Amber and Red, the braces show a list. The card shows only the items that apply, with " · " between them.

**The disclaimer**, on the settings page and at the first enable:

> Labels describe what Viewpoint's automatic check found in this version of the addon's Java code. They are not a promise of safety: a check can miss things, and an addon can misbehave within what it is allowed. Addons are made by third parties. Viewpoint's authors do not review, endorse or answer for them.

**Unmanaged**, amber:

> Unmanaged: runs outside Viewpoint's controls (hooks cannot be listed, ordered or vetoed)

Some Unmanaged mods are red. Then the card adds **loads before Viewpoint**, or a different reason.

**A resource pack**:

> Resource pack: assets only. Viewpoint read these files with its own loaders and found them within its limits. It contains no Java.

**A Shaderpack**:

> Shaderpack: GLSL only. It contains no Java.

The card also shows the licence of the pack, or **No licence given**.

**The shader line**:

> Has shader code: Viewpoint checks its size and form. Faulty shader code can stall or crash the graphics driver.

**The Lua line**, on each label: **Has Lua: not checked by Viewpoint**, or **No Lua**.

> **Note**
>
> When you describe your addon to players, tell them what it does and what it asks for. Do not call it safe because its
> label is Normal.

## Consent

The player gives consent to one **version** of one package. There is no "allow all". If an update asks for more, the
player must give consent again. See [Updates & changelogs](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/trust/updates-and-changelogs.md).

---

# Updates & changelogs

> Which updates need consent again, which only show a dot, and how to write a useful changelog.

The player gives consent to one version of a package. When the package changes, Viewpoint compares it with the version
that the player accepted. If the new version asks for more, the player must give consent again.

## What needs consent again

After one of these changes, the package stays **off** until the player gives consent again. This is also true if the
package was active before.

| Change | Consent again |
| --- | --- |
| A higher label level, or a new Amber or Red reason | Yes |
| A new permission | Yes |
| A new class in `hooks.targets` | Yes |
| A new hooked member of Viewpoint | Yes |
| A new hook, or a stronger kind (`OBSERVE` < `ARGS` < `RETURN` < `SKIP`) | Yes |
| A new host in `downloads.hosts` | Yes |
| A larger `files.quotaMiB` | Yes |
| A new kind of asset | Yes |
| A new Lua file, or a new item in the Lua line | Yes |
| `side` changes from `client` to `gameplay` | Yes |
| A new package in `requires` | Yes |
| A new export (`@LuaExport`) or a new Lua global | Yes |
| A new snippet point or a new draw point | Yes |
| A new claim kind: camera, view, shot resolver, reticle or cursor | Yes |
| A new package in `exports` | Yes |
| A new member of Viewpoint that the addon uses, reflects or hooks | Yes |
| For a Shaderpack: a new `base`, or a new package in `requires` | Yes |
| A signature that is removed or changed | Yes |
| Other changes, for example GLSL code that changes with no change of level | No. The card shows a dot. |

A package that needs consent again never starts without it. This is also true after a restart. A Red addon asks for its
second confirmation each time.

## The dot

Each change puts a **dot** on the card, also when the package is off. A package that you never accepted has no dot:
there is nothing to compare it with. To read what changed, click **Info** and open the **Changelog** tab. The dot goes when
you accept the package, or when you open **Info** for a package that your consent still covers. It does not go
when the package only starts, also not at the start of the game: a package that your consent covers starts, and the dot
stays until you have seen what changed. Opening **Info** for a package that asks for more does not give consent.
The **Changelog** tab shows:

1. the changelog, from the accepted version to the new version;
2. the changes, in these groups: permissions; hooks and the parts of Viewpoint that the package uses; exports, drawing
   and claims; downloads, files and requirements; the label, its reasons and the signature; assets, Lua and shader
   code; the package itself (its version, its descriptor and its jar).

Each change that asks for more has a mark. The card also says why it is off, for example: *An update asks for more than
you accepted. It stays off until you accept it.*

## When an update has an effect

Viewpoint starts a package from the files that it found at that time. Files that it finds later apply at the next
enable. An addon also keeps the jar that it loaded, in memory: a jar that you replace on the disk cannot change what
runs. The card shows *Update available. It applies at the next enable or restart.* It shows this also when only the jar
changed and the descriptor is the same. The next enable reads the new files, and compares them with the player's consent.
A new package always starts **Inactive**.

An update that asks for more never starts by itself. If the package runs, the old version goes on running, and the card
says that the update applies when the player switches the package on again and accepts it. If the package is off, it
stays off, also at the next start of the game, until the player accepts it.

## Write a changelog

Name the file with `changelog=CHANGELOG.md`:

```markdown title="CHANGELOG.md"
## 1.2.0

Lean now eases in over a quarter of a second.
It asks for the `downloads` permission to fetch the curve table (github.com).

## 1.1.0

Fixed the lean snapping when the player turns.
```

Rules:

- Start each section with `## <version>`, for example `## 1.2.0`. Text after the version on the same line, for example a
  date, is allowed. A short version such as `## 1.2` is the same as `## 1.2.0`. A heading such as `## v1.2` or
  `## [1.2.0]` has no version that Viewpoint can read, so Viewpoint does not show its section.
- Viewpoint shows only the sections with a version that is newer than the one that the player accepted, and not newer
  than the new version. If Viewpoint does not know the version that the player accepted, it shows every section up to the
  new version. It does not show text before the first section, or a section with no version.
- Viewpoint reads the first 64 KiB of the file and shows at most 8000 characters. Put the newest section first: the
  rest of a longer file is not read.
- Viewpoint shows the text as **plain text**. It shows links, but does not open them. It removes control characters and
  format characters, for example right-to-left overrides and zero-width characters.
- Write what changed for the player.
- If you ask for more, write what you added and why. The player reads this line before they decide.

> **Tip**
>
> A good changelog does not remove the consent dialog. It tells the player why you need more. Then the player can decide
> quickly.

---

# ZombieBuddy policy & signatures

> How the ZombieBuddy policy and an optional .zbs signature affect an addon.

ZombieBuddy loads Viewpoint and each mod that has `javaJarFile`. Viewpoint loads addons. Viewpoint obeys two ZombieBuddy
settings: the policy, and the signatures. No other ZombieBuddy approval applies to addons.

## The ZombieBuddy policy

ZombieBuddy has a policy for jars that the player has not approved: `prompt`, `deny-new` or `allow-all`. Viewpoint reads
it one time, when the game starts.

| Policy | Addons with Java |
| --- | --- |
| `deny-new`, a policy that Viewpoint does not know, or a policy that Viewpoint cannot read | **Cannot start.** The card gives the cause. Resource packs continue to work. |
| `allow-all` or `prompt` | Viewpoint's consent controls the start. |

Only these two policies hand the decision to the player. A newer, stricter ZombieBuddy policy stops the addons until
Viewpoint knows it. Viewpoint is never more permissive than ZombieBuddy.

With `allow-all`, ZombieBuddy ignores the setting for unsigned mods and the `.zbs` file. Viewpoint does not: it still
applies the rules below to each addon, and a `.zbs` that is not correct still stops it.

## An optional signature

You can put a `.zbs` file next to the jar, with the name of the jar: `lean.jar.zbs`. Viewpoint checks it with the
ZombieBuddy signature check.

| The `.zbs` file | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Is correct | The **Trust** tab shows *Signed by X*. |
| Is not correct | The addon **never starts**. |
| Cannot be checked now, for example when the computer is offline | The addon does not start. The card says **its signature could not be checked**. Click **Rescan** to try again. Viewpoint also tries again after a minute. |
| Is missing | The **Trust** tab shows *Unsigned*. If ZombieBuddy refuses unsigned mods, the addon does not start. |

The check reads the Steam profile of the signer, and this can take some seconds. Viewpoint does it in the background. The
card shows **Checking** until it is done, and the game does not wait. For the rest of the session, Viewpoint keeps the
keys it fetched, so the next jar of the same signer needs no new request. For the authors in the ZombieBuddy list,
Viewpoint takes the keys from that list (ZombieBuddy keeps a copy on the disk), so a computer that is offline can still
check their jars. If a signer changes their key, Viewpoint asks Steam once more. If a signer revokes a key, a jar that
was checked with it stays valid until you restart the game. The `.zbs` file must be in the package's folder, and it must
be smaller than 64 KiB.

*X* is the SteamID64 that the `.zbs` file declares, and the file is correct for that SteamID64. Viewpoint does not
compare it with the account that uploaded the mod to the Workshop. A signature tells who signed the file. It does not
tell who uploaded it, and it does not tell what the file does.

## What does not apply

- Viewpoint's label is not a ZombieBuddy approval. A ZombieBuddy approval is not a label.
- The ZombieBuddy approval of a jar does not apply to addons.
- The ZombieBuddy list of authors that the player trusts does not apply to addons. Viewpoint uses only the keys in it, to
  check a signature.

## For addon authors

- Do not set `javaJarFile` for an addon.
- If you have a ZombieBuddy build and an addon build of the same code, give them different mod ids.
- Do not refer to ZombieBuddy from an addon. Viewpoint refuses the jar. This includes `WatchesAPI`.
- Two ZombieBuddy annotations are the exception. Viewpoint reads `@Patch` and `@Exposer.LuaClass` in an addon jar and
  runs them as hooks and as exports. See [Migrating from ZombieBuddy](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/patching/migrating-from-zombiebuddy.md).
- A Shaderpack has no jar. ZombieBuddy has no part in it.

> **Note**
>
> A signature is optional. If you sign, you must sign each new version of the jar. A signature that is not correct stops
> the addon.

---

# Assets & budgets

> The memory pools of your assets, the estimates of their cost, and what occurs when a pool is full.

Viewpoint keeps assets in memory pools. Each pool has a maximum size. Viewpoint counts your assets in the pools for your
package. The card shows your part. If a pool is full, Viewpoint refuses *your* next asset. It never removes the assets
of a different package to make space.

## The pools

| Asset | Pool | Default size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Models | `memory.packMiB` (video memory) | 768 MiB |
| Textures | `memory.packMiB` (video memory) | 768 MiB, together with models |
| Sounds | `memory.soundMiB` | 128 MiB |
| Data files (16 MiB maximum each) | `memory.addonDataMiB` (memory) | 64 MiB |
| Shader snippets, Lua exports and the text of Shaderpacks | `memory.addonDataMiB` (memory), together with data files | 64 MiB |
| Buffers and textures that you make with `Gpu` | `draw.gpuMiB` (video memory), for each addon | 64 MiB by default; you set the amount, more than 128 MiB with the permission `vram` |
| Tile textures | `memory.texturePackMiB` (video memory), and `memory.texturePackDiskMiB` on disk | 256 MiB, 1024 MiB |

The player can change the pool sizes in Viewpoint's settings, on the **World**, **Memory** page.

Tile textures are different. If the tile packs that the player selects need more, Viewpoint increases their pools, and
`memory.floorMiB` and `memory.wallMiB`, so that the tiles keep all their detail. See [Tiles](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/tiles.md).

If there is no space for your icon, the card shows a tile with a letter.

## Estimates

The **Performance** tab shows an estimate before the package loads. Viewpoint calculates it from the file headers when
the tab opens.

| What | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Video memory, textures | width × height × 4 bytes × 4/3 (with mipmaps) |
| Video memory, models | vertices × the vertex size + indices × 4 bytes |
| Memory, data | the file size |
| Memory, sounds | sample rate × channels × 2 bytes × duration |
| Memory, classes | approximately 3 × the class bytes in the jar |
| Video memory, targets of a Shaderpack | the targets that the pack declares × the size of the output × the size of the format |
| Main-thread time, for each hook | calls each frame × the measured cost of one call, or *unknown until measured* |
| Graphics-card time | *measured only* |

A texture of 2048 × 2048 pixels uses approximately 21 MiB with mipmaps. A texture of 4096 × 4096 pixels uses 85 MiB.

## When a pool is full

The video memory of the `Gpu` objects works in a different way. Your addon asks for an amount in `draw.gpuMiB`, and
Viewpoint gives it when the addon starts:

- Viewpoint sets no limit on the amount. The graphics card of the player is the limit. The card of your addon shows the
  amount to the player, and more than 128 MiB needs the permission `vram`.
- When your addon asks for a buffer or a texture past its own amount, the call fails, and the message names
  `draw.gpuMiB`.
- Viewpoint frees all your `Gpu` objects when the addon goes off.

- The load of that asset fails.
- The error names the pool. The card shows the same error.
- Your other assets stay loaded.

To correct this, release an asset that you do not use. Or ask the player to make the pool larger.

## Where the work occurs

Viewpoint decodes your assets on a different thread. It counts that time for your package. Viewpoint sends the assets to
the graphics card a little each frame. Viewpoint reads and parses a Shaderpack on this thread also.

## Keep it small

- Load an asset when you need it. Release it when you do not need it.
- Use one texture for many models.
- Use one texture of 1024 × 1024 pixels in place of four textures of 512 × 512 pixels that you always use together.
- Use `ogg` for long sounds.

> **Note**
>
> The estimates are approximate. The **Performance** tab shows them next to the measured values. See
> [Measuring your addon](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/performance/measuring-your-addon.md).

---

# Measuring your addon

> What the Performance tab and Viewpoint's profiler show about an addon, and how to measure its graphics cost.

The game is usually limited by the processor, not by the graphics card. Viewpoint shows the cost of each package to
the player. You can use the same values.

## The Performance tab

On the card of a package, open **Info**, then **Performance**.

| Row | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Assets | The assets by kind, and their sizes |
| Video memory | The estimate and the measured value |
| Memory | The estimate and the measured value |
| Processor | The time of your hooks on the main thread, the time of your work on the render thread, and the time of your work on other threads |
| Graphics card | The time of your draw callbacks and your shader snippets, as measured by Viewpoint. For a Shaderpack: the time of each pass. |
| History | The average and the range for the last 8 sessions |

The measured values:

- **Main thread:** the time of your handlers. Viewpoint measures a sample of the calls, and calculates the total.
  The profiler counter `addon.<id>.mainMs` gets the value each frame.
- **Render thread:** the time of your draw callbacks and your `RENDER` hooks. The profiler counter `addon.<id>.renderMs`
  gets the value each frame.
- **Graphics card:** the time of the work that your addon asks the graphics card for, at each draw point, in
  `addon.<id>.gpuMs`. If two addons put a snippet in the same shader, Viewpoint can time only that shader. The card then
  says "shared with N". Use **Measure GPU cost** to find the cost of each addon.
- **Other threads:** the time to decode your assets.
- **Memory and video memory:** the bytes of your package in the pools.

Viewpoint measures the time of draw callbacks. It cannot measure the time of your assets or your snippets one by one. To
find that cost, do the measurement below.

## Measure the graphics cost

1. Go to a scene where the game shows your assets.
2. On the **Performance** tab, click **Measure GPU cost**.
3. Do not move. The game shows **measuring, keep still**.
4. Wait. Viewpoint compares frames with your assets and your snippets on and off, 10 times.
5. Read the result on the tab. Viewpoint keeps the median difference, with the date.

## Shaderpacks

The card of a Shaderpack shows two values.

- **Video memory:** an estimate of the targets that the pack declares. It is the number of targets, times the size of the
  output, times the size of the format.
- **Time on the graphics card:** the time of each pass of the pack, measured while the pack is in use.

**Measure against base** is planned. It can come after API 1.0. It compares your pack with the pack that it builds on, in
the same scene. Use it to see what your changes cost.

## History

Viewpoint keeps the history in `Zomboid/viewpoint-addons/_manager/usage.properties`. It keeps the last 8 sessions for
each package, and the session that is still running. It removes a package that it has not seen for 90 days.

A session holds only: the day it ended (not the time), the number of frames to the nearest thousand, the mean time on the
main thread, the memory and video memory that the package held, how many assets it held, and the first eight characters of
the hash of its jar. Viewpoint writes the file every five minutes while you play and when the game exits. The file stays on
the player's computer and nothing sends it anywhere. It is in the cache folder that players often zip for a bug report: a
player can delete it at any time.

## Viewpoint's profiler

Your hooks, your draw callbacks and your work on the render thread show in Viewpoint's profiler, in the group `ADDONS`. Open the *Profiling* page or the profiler window.
Compare a frame with your addon on and a frame with your addon off.

An addon with no active hooks, no callbacks and no assets adds no cost to the frame.

> **Tip**
>
> Measure in the scenes where the game is slowest: a street with many zombies, a car that moves, rain. A hook that costs
> 0.05 ms in an empty field can cost ten times more in a mall.

---

# Format

> The folders of a resource pack, the version 2 model manifest, and the limits of the files.

A resource pack contains assets and no code. `pack.properties` describes it. It can have four kinds of asset.

- media/viewpoint/resourcepacks/example.pack/
  - pack.properties
  - icon.png
  - models/
    - manifest.txt
    - crate.obj
    - crate.mtl
    - crate.png
    - chair.obj
    - chair.mtl
    - chair.png
  - tiles/
  - sounds/
  - data/

```properties title="pack.properties"
format=1
id=example.pack
name=Example pack
version=1.0.0
author=Example
game.min=42.21
models=models/manifest.txt
tiles=tiles
sounds=sounds
data=data
```

`models` is the path of the manifest file. `tiles`, `sounds` and `data` are folders. Each path is relative to the
folder of the pack, and must be in the folder of the pack's version or in `common/` (the folder that holds its
`media` folder). The [Descriptor](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/concepts/descriptor.md) page gives the common keys.

## Models

The manifest is a text file of `key=value` lines. Put `format=2` in it: this is version 2, the version for all new packs.
If Viewpoint cannot read a line, it ignores that line, and names its line number in the log. It uses the other lines.

```properties title="models/manifest.txt"
format=2
id=example.pack
name=Example pack

model.crate=crate.obj
model.chair=chair.obj

bind.furniture_storage_01_5=crate,90,0,0,0,1.0
group.furniture_seating_indoor_02/Wooden Chair=chair,0,0,0.1,0,1
```

| Line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `format=2` | The version of the manifest. |
| `id`, `name` | The id and name of the manifest, for messages. |
| `model.<id>=<path>` | A model: an OBJ file, relative to the folder of the manifest. Viewpoint finds its MTL and PNG files from the OBJ file. |
| `group.<tileset>/<name>=<model>,<degrees>,<x>,<y>,<z>,<scale>` | One line for all the facings of an object. See [Group binds](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/model-states.md#group-binds). |
| `bind.<sprite>=<model>,<degrees>,<x>,<y>,<z>,<scale>` | The sprite whose square shows this model, the model id, its rotation in degrees, its offset and its scale. A bind is stronger than a group in the same pack. |

> **Note**
>
> The two `format` keys are different. In `pack.properties`, `format=1` is the version of the descriptor. In the manifest,
> `format=2` is the version of the manifest.

The model stands on its square:

- The origin is the **centre** of the square.
- The axes are `x` east, `y` south, `z` up. One storey is the side of a square multiplied by √6.
- The model turns about the vertical axis by its degrees, from east towards south. Then it moves by its offset.

The model replaces the art of the sprite: the projected art, the game's own sprite model, or the card of a plant.
Viewpoint loads a model the first time that the game shows its sprite. When two packs put a model on the same sprite,
the pack nearer the top of the Active column wins.

A model can change its parts when its object is lit. See [Model states](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/model-states.md).

Each material of the MTL uses the PNG of its `map_Kd` line. When the materials of a model use more than one PNG,
Viewpoint puts these PNGs together on one texture as it loads the model. Together, they must fit in 2056 × 2056
pixels. If they are larger, Viewpoint makes each of them half as large (again, if necessary) and writes a line in the
log. Keep the UVs of a model in the range 0 to 1: a model does not repeat its texture.

### Version 1 (legacy)

> **Caution**
>
> Version 1 is deprecated. Do not use it for a new pack.

A manifest without `format=2` is version 1. Viewpoint continues to read it. Version 1 has only `bind.` lines: one line
for each sprite. Viewpoint ignores its `group.` lines, and the log names them. To change a pack to version 2, see
[Migrate to version 2](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/migrating.md).

This is not the *legacy* flag on a card. That flag shows a pack that its Lua registers, with no descriptor. See
[Legacy model packs](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/legacy-model-packs.md).

## Tiles

Tile textures have their own format. See [Tiles](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/tiles.md).

## Sounds

`ogg` and `wav` files. The **Performance** line of the card includes them. In this version, Viewpoint does not play the
sounds of a resource pack, and they do not replace the sounds of the game. To play a sound, put it in an addon. See
[Assets](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/assets.md).

## Data

Read-only files. Viewpoint does not use them itself. An addon reads only the data of its own package. See
[Assets](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/assets.md). The Lua of the mod can read them with the file functions of the game.

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| One data file | 16 MiB |
| All assets | They count in their pool. If the pool is full, Viewpoint refuses the asset, and the card tells you. |
| Paths | In the folder of the pack's version or in `common/`, the one that holds its `media` folder. Viewpoint refuses an absolute path, a `\`, and a link or a junction that goes out of it. A `..` is allowed when the file stays in that folder. |

If Viewpoint cannot read a file, the card names the file. See [Labels](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/trust/labels.md#resource-packs-and-shaderpacks).

> **Note**
>
> A resource pack has no Java and no shader code. If you need Java, make an addon. If you need to change how the whole
> frame is drawn, make a [Shaderpack](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/shaderpacks/format.md). Viewpoint does not check the Lua of the
> mod. The last line of the label tells the player this.

---

# Model states

> One model for all the states of an object. Name the parts that change when the object is lit, make a part glow, and bind all the facings of an object with one line.

An object can change while the game runs. A lamp goes on and off. You do not make a model for each state. You make
**one model**, and you name the **parts** that change. Viewpoint shows the parts for the state of the object. When the
state changes, Viewpoint changes the parts at once. It does not load a second model.

A version 2 manifest also has **group binds**: one line for all the facings of an object.

To change a version 1 pack, see [Migrate to version 2](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/migrating.md).

## Parts

Your OBJ file has objects (`o`) or groups (`g`). Put a tag in the name of an object or a group:

| Tag in the name | The part shows |
| --- | --- |
| `[lit]` | Only when the object is lit. |
| `[!lit]` | Only when the object is not lit. |
| No tag | Always. |

```text title="lamp.obj"
mtllib lamp.mtl
o Base
usemtl wood
f ...
o Shade[!lit]
usemtl shade
f ...
o Shade[lit]
usemtl shade_on
f ...
```

- To change the look of a part, put the part two times in the model: one time with `[!lit]` and one time with `[lit]`.
  The two copies can have a different shape, or different UVs on your texture.
- Make only the parts that change. The other parts are shared by all the states.
- The tag can be anywhere in the name. `Shade[lit]_Mesh.001` is correct.
- The tag of a group (`g`) is more important than the tag of its object (`o`).
- A name with both tags shows in all the states, as a name with no tag.

## Glow

A material glows when your MTL gives it an emission colour that is not black (`Ke`), or an emission map (`map_Ke`).
A part that glows is drawn as bright as its texture, without the light of the scene: a bulb, a screen, a flame.

```text title="lamp.mtl"
newmtl shade
map_Kd lamp.png

newmtl shade_on
Ke 1.0 0.85 0.6
map_Kd lamp.png
```

Blender writes `Ke` when the material has an emission colour. Use a glowing material only on a `[lit]` part, or the
part glows in all the states.

> **Note**
>
> Each material uses the texture of its own `map_Kd`. The two copies of a part can use different materials, with
> different textures. A model that uses one texture for all its states uses less memory. See
> [Format](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/format.md).

## Lit

An object is lit when:

| Object | Lit when |
| --- | --- |
| A lamp or a light switch | It is on and it has power: a battery, electricity on its square, or the power grid. A street lamp is lit only at night. |
| A stove, an oven or a microwave | It is on. |
| A generator | It is on. |
| A radio or a television | It is on. |
| A fireplace or a barbecue | It burns. |

Any other object is never lit, and its `[lit]` parts never show. When an object changes, Viewpoint shows the other
parts in a short time (about a tenth of a second).

## Group binds

A group bind gives the same model to all the facings of an object:

```properties title="models/manifest.txt"
format=2
model.chair=chair.obj
group.furniture_seating_indoor_02/Wooden Chair=chair,0,0,0.1,0,1
```

| Line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `group.<tileset>/<name>=<model>,<degrees>,<x>,<y>,<z>,<scale>` | The model of each facing of the object. `<tileset>` is the sheet of the sprites, for example `furniture_seating_indoor_02`. `<name>` is the name of the object: its `GroupName`, a space, and its `CustomName`, for example `Wooden Chair`. If the object has no `GroupName`, use its `CustomName`. The values are the same as in a bind. |

You make the model for the object that **faces south**. Viewpoint turns the model to the `Facing` of each sprite:
south 0 degrees, west 90, north 180, east 270. It turns the offset `<x>,<y>` together with the model. Thus a model that
you move back against the wall of a south-facing chair stays against the wall when the chair faces east.

- A bind of a sprite (`bind.<sprite>=`) is stronger than the bind of its group, in the same pack.
- An object that has more than one square (its sprites have a `SpriteGridPos`) does not get a group bind. Bind each of
  its sprites.
- If a group finds no sprite, the log names the group.
- Without `format=2`, Viewpoint ignores group lines, and the log names them.

## Other states

Open, closed, damaged and facing are not states of a model. In the game, each of them is a different sprite: an open
door, a smashed window, each facing of a chair. Bind that sprite. A bind cannot have a state in its key: Viewpoint
ignores `bind.<sprite>[lit]=` and names the line in the log.

## Rules

- See [Format](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/format.md#models) for how a model stands on its square.
- Models count in `memory.packMiB`. Viewpoint loads a model the first time that the game shows it.
- The package nearer the top of the Active column wins a sprite. See [Order](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/concepts/order.md).
- A line that Viewpoint cannot read is ignored. The log names its line number.

> **Note**
>
> A model with parts works in an older Viewpoint too: there, all its parts show at the same time. A version 2 manifest
> needs a Viewpoint that supports it. An older Viewpoint ignores its group lines.

For a model that needs code, see [Model providers](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/model-providers.md).

---

# Tiles

> Replace the game's tile art with your own, with normal and specular textures, as one PNG for each tile.

The `tiles` folder of a resource pack replaces the art of the game's tiles: floors, walls, furniture, plants. While the
pack is active, Viewpoint shows your PNG in place of the game's art. The isometric view of the game keeps its own art.

## One PNG for each tile

Give each file the id of the tile in the game, as the game's tile sheets name it:

- tiles/
  - walls_exterior_house_01_0.png
  - walls_exterior_house_01_0_n.png
  - walls_exterior_house_01_0_s.png

| File | Contains | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<id>.png` | The colour | Yes |
| `<id>_n.png` | The normal texture, in the LabPBR layout | No |
| `<id>_s.png` | The specular texture, in the LabPBR layout | No |

If you give `<id>_n` or `<id>_s`, the light uses the surface of your tile. If you do not, Viewpoint lights the tile as it
lights the game's art. `<id>_n` and `<id>_s` must have the same size as `<id>`.

## The size and the shape of a tile

Your tiles are made for Viewpoint, so floors and walls are flat: do not draw them at the isometric angle of the game.

| Tile | The art | Sizes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A floor | A square, seen from above. North is at the top. | 64 × 64, 128 × 128 or 256 × 256 |
| A wall | One face, seen from the side that the game shows: from the south for a north wall, from the east for a west wall. The bottom row is on the floor. | 64 × 192, 128 × 384 or 256 × 768 |
| A corner of two walls | The north face, then the west face, side by side. | 128 × 192, 256 × 384 or 512 × 768 |
| All other tiles | The full frame of the tile, as the tile sheets of the game give it, for example 128 × 256. | The frame, or 2 or 4 times its size |

The larger sizes give more detail when the player is near. Viewpoint does not use a PNG of another size, and writes in
the log the sizes that the tile can have.

Many Minecraft resource packs use LabPBR for normals, smoothness, reflectance and emission. Textures in that layout
work here with no change.

## How Viewpoint uses them

- Viewpoint puts many tiles together on large textures. It keeps them on disk, so the next start is faster. When you
  change a PNG, Viewpoint reads it again.
- If the game has no tile with the name of a PNG, Viewpoint writes it in the log and does not use the PNG.
- A floor tile also replaces the ceilings that show the art of that floor.
- The far world shows your tiles too. From far away, a tile shows the average colour of your PNG.
- When the player changes the packs, the far world goes and Viewpoint builds it again from the new tiles. This can take
  some seconds. Viewpoint keeps the result on disk, so the next time it is faster.
- The game tints its grass floors. It also tints your tile for a grass floor.
- They count in `memory.texturePackMiB` (256 MiB by default). The disk copy counts in `memory.texturePackDiskMiB`
  (1024 MiB by default). If your tiles need more, Viewpoint increases these sizes, so that all your tiles show. When the
  player switches the pack off, Viewpoint makes them smaller again.
- The default shader pack and Iris shader packs both use them.

## Estimates

A tile of width `w` and height `h` uses approximately `w × h × 4 × 4/3` bytes of video memory for each texture, with
mipmaps. Before the player switches the pack on, the **Performance** tab shows the total.

Viewpoint also bakes floors and ceilings into pages. For floors of 128 × 128, the pages can use 4 times the video memory
that they use for the art of the game. For floors of 256 × 256, they can use 16 times that memory, up to about 6 GiB.
Viewpoint increases the pool `memory.floorMiB` by this amount, so that your floors keep all their detail.

Viewpoint also bakes walls into arrays, in `memory.wallMiB`. With walls of 256 × 768, these can use up to about 2 GiB.

## Order

When two packs have the same tile, the pack nearer the top of the Active column wins, for each tile. See
[Order](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/concepts/order.md).

---

# Legacy model packs

> How older model packs load, and how to change one into a resource pack.

An older model pack is a mod whose Lua registers a manifest:

```lua
Viewpoint.ModelPacks.register("MyPackMod", "media/models/pack.txt")
```

These packs continue to work. Viewpoint shows each one as a resource pack with the **legacy** flag.

## How Viewpoint finds a legacy pack

Viewpoint reads the Lua of each enabled mod. It looks for calls to `Viewpoint.ModelPacks.register("<modId>", "<path>")`
whose two arguments are fixed strings. For each call, it shows a resource pack:

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Id | `legacy.<modId>` |
| Version and game range | From the `mod.info` of the mod |
| Models | The manifest of the call, in the version folder of the mod, then in `common/` |
| Flag | *legacy* |

If your Lua makes the path while the game runs, Viewpoint cannot find the call when it reads the Lua. When the call
occurs, Viewpoint shows the pack as **registered at run time**.

## What is different

- A legacy pack follows the player's **order** and **switch**. The pack nearer the top of the Active column wins a
  sprite. Before, the pack that registered last won.
- Viewpoint moves the old switch of each pack (`packs.<modId>`) into the **Graphics**, **Resource Packs** page one time. A pack that was on
  starts **Active**. A pack that was off starts **Inactive**. The pack that registered last goes to the top.
- The manifest, the models and their art must be in the folder of the version or in `common/`, the one that holds the
  `media` folder of the pack. If a path goes outside (with `..`, an absolute path, a `\` or a link), Viewpoint refuses
  it and names it in `console.txt`. Move the files into that folder.
- A legacy pack has no descriptor. Thus its card has no author, no icon and no changelog, other than what `mod.info`
  gives.

## Change it into a resource pack

1. Make the file `media/viewpoint/resourcepacks/<id>/pack.properties`.
2. Write the common keys in it.
3. Add `models=` with the path of your manifest.
4. Move the manifest and its models into that folder, or set `models=` to their current path.
5. Remove the call to `Viewpoint.ModelPacks.register`.
6. Add a version, an author and an icon.

The manifest does not change in these steps. Then change it to version 2. See
[Migrate to version 2](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/migrating.md).

> **Note**
>
> Legacy packs continue to work, but do not make a new pack in this way. See [Format](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/format.md). A resource pack can also have an icon, a version, a
> changelog, tiles, sounds and data.

---

# Migrate to version 2

> Change an older model pack into a resource pack, replace the lines of each facing with one group bind, and join the models of the states of an object into one model.

Version 1 manifests and older model packs are deprecated. They continue to work. A new pack starts at version 2: see
[Format](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/format.md). This page tells you how to change an existing pack, one step at a time. You can stop
after any step.

| Step | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Make a resource pack | A card with a version, an author and an icon. The player sees what the pack contains. |
| 2. Use group binds | One line for all the facings of an object, in place of one line for each sprite. |
| 3. Join the state models | One model for a lamp that is on and off. It uses less memory, and it changes at once. |

## 1. Make a resource pack

An older pack is a mod whose Lua calls `Viewpoint.ModelPacks.register`. Viewpoint shows it as a *legacy* pack.

1. Make the file `media/viewpoint/resourcepacks/<id>/pack.properties`. See [Descriptor](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/concepts/descriptor.md) for the
   id and the common keys.
2. Add `models=` with the path of your manifest. The path is relative to the folder of the pack.
3. Move the manifest, the OBJ, MTL and PNG files into the folder of the pack, or set `models=` to their current path.
   All the files must stay in the folder of the version of your mod or in `common/`.
4. Remove the call to `Viewpoint.ModelPacks.register` from your Lua.
5. Start the game. Open **Graphics**, **Resource Packs**. Your pack shows as a resource pack, without the *legacy* flag.

```properties title="media/viewpoint/resourcepacks/example.pack/pack.properties"
format=1
id=example.pack
name=Example pack
version=1.0.0
author=Example
game.min=42.21
models=models/manifest.txt
```

The manifest does not change. For more, see [Legacy model packs](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/legacy-model-packs.md).

## 2. Use group binds

A piece of furniture has a sprite for each facing. A version 1 manifest has a line for each sprite, each with its own
turn:

```properties title="Before: version 1"
model.chair=chair.obj
bind.furniture_seating_indoor_02_0=chair,0,0,0,0,1
bind.furniture_seating_indoor_02_1=chair,270,0,0,0,1
bind.furniture_seating_indoor_02_2=chair,180,0,0,0,1
bind.furniture_seating_indoor_02_3=chair,90,0,0,0,1
```

```properties title="After: version 2"
format=2
model.chair=chair.obj
group.furniture_seating_indoor_02/Wooden Chair=chair,0,0,0,0,1
```

1. Add `format=2` to the manifest.
2. Find the name of the object: its `GroupName` and its `CustomName` in the properties of its tiles (TileZed shows
   them). Write them with a space between them, for example `Wooden Chair`.
3. Find the line of the sprite that faces south. Copy its model and values into one `group.<tileset>/<name>=` line,
   with the turn of the south-facing sprite.
4. Remove the lines of the other facings.
5. Start the game. The log says how many sprites the groups of your pack bind:
   `model pack example.pack: its groups bind 4 sprites`.

- Keep a `bind.` line for a sprite whose model is different. It is stronger than the group.
- If your model is not made to face south, add its turn to the group line. For a model that faces east, the turn is 90.
- If the log says `no single-square sprite in ...`, the name is wrong, or the object has more than one square. Keep a
  `bind.` line for each sprite of an object that has more than one square.

## 3. Join the state models

If your pack has two models for one object, for example a lamp that is off and the same lamp with a bright shade, a
bind can show only one of them. Put the two looks into one model.

1. Open the two models in your editor, for example Blender. Import the second model into the scene of the first.
2. Delete the parts of the second model that are the same as the first: the base, the stand.
3. Rename the parts that change. Add `[!lit]` to the name of the part from the off model, for example `Shade[!lit]`.
   Add `[lit]` to the name of the part from the on model, for example `Shade[lit]`.
4. Keep the materials and the textures of the two models: each material uses the texture of its own `map_Kd`. To use
   less memory, put the two textures into one texture, in different areas, and move the UVs of each part into its area.
5. For a part that must glow, give its material an emission colour. Blender writes it as `Ke` in the MTL.
6. Export one OBJ and one MTL. Make sure that the OBJ keeps the names of the parts: each part starts with a line
   `o <name>` or `g <name>`. Blender writes `o <name>` for each object.
7. In the manifest, remove the second model and its binds. Keep one bind, to the joined model.

```text title="lamp.obj, after"
mtllib lamp.mtl
o Base
f ...
o Shade[!lit]
f ...
o Shade[lit]
f ...
```

Check it in the game: switch the lamp on and off. The shade changes in about a tenth of a second. If both shades show
at the same time, the names do not have the tags, or a name has both tags.

> **Tip**
>
> Only the parts that change are in the model two times. A lamp that changes only its shade costs the shade two times,
> not the whole lamp. See [Model states](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/resource-packs/model-states.md) for the objects that can be lit.

## What to check

| Check | Where |
| --- | --- |
| The pack shows as a resource pack, not *legacy* | **Graphics**, **Resource Packs** |
| No line of the manifest is ignored | `console.txt`: `model pack <id>: ... lines left out` names each one |
| The groups bind the sprites you expect | `console.txt`: `its groups bind N sprites` |
| The textures of a model fit together | `console.txt`: `drawn at 1/N size` shows when they are too large |

---

# Format

> The folder of a Shaderpack, the keys of its pack.properties, options, presets, the pipeline, and how packs build on each other.

A Shaderpack changes how Viewpoint draws the world: its light, its sky, its colours, and which effects run. It is a
folder of GLSL files and one `pack.properties`. It has no Java. The player chooses one Shaderpack at a time on the
Graphics page.

- media/viewpoint/shaderpacks/example.dusk/
  - pack.properties
  - icon.png
  - CHANGELOG.md
  - shaders/
    - lib/shade.glsl
    - post.frag
  - textures/

- The folder name must be the same as the `id`.
- `shaders/` holds your GLSL files. See [Library files](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/shaderpacks/library-files.md).
- `textures/` is optional. It holds the images that your shaders read.
- One mod can hold many Shaderpacks.
- The id of the package is also the id of the pack.

## The descriptor

```properties title="pack.properties"
format=1
id=example.dusk
name=Dusk
version=1.0.0
author=Example
description=The default look with a warmer grade and softer shadows.
icon=icon.png
license=MIT
game.min=42.21
base=default
changelog=CHANGELOG.md

options=warmth grain
option.warmth.label=Warmth
option.warmth.tooltip=How much the grade leans towards orange.
option.warmth.range=0 1 0.05
option.warmth.default=0.4

option.grain.label=Film grain
option.grain.default=false

presets=fast balanced
preset.default=balanced
preset.fast.label=Fast
preset.fast=warmth=0 grain=false
preset.balanced=

pipeline.bloom=true
pipeline.shadowCascades=2
```

The file is a Java properties file in UTF-8. A long value can go on over several lines with `\` at the end of each line.
A Shaderpack has no `jar`, `entry`, `api` or `permissions` key, because it has no code.

### Package keys

These keys are the same as in the other descriptors. See [Descriptor](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/concepts/descriptor.md).

| Key | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `format`, `id`, `name`, `version` | Yes | As for all packages. |
| `game.min` | Yes | The oldest game build. |
| `game.max`, `viewpoint.min`, `viewpoint.max` | No | The ranges that you tested. |
| `author`, `description`, `icon`, `license`, `changelog` | No | Shown on the card. The card shows the licence, or **No licence given**. |
| `requires`, `conflicts` | No | Other packages. A package that is your `base` must be in `requires`. |
| `library` | No | The Viewpoint version that you made the pack for (planned). See [Library files](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/shaderpacks/library-files.md#made-for-a-version). |

### Pack keys

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `base` | The pack that yours starts from: its files, options and pipeline. If you leave it out, the pack starts from the library alone. See [Build on another pack](#build-on-another-pack). |
| `dropOptions` | The options of the base that your pack leaves out, by id. They are gone from the window, and their defines are not set. |
| `options` | The ids of your own options, in the order that the window lists them. |
| `presets` | The ids of your own presets, in the order of the **Quality** list. |
| `preset.default` | The preset that a new install starts with. |
| `passes`, `pass.<id>.*`, `targets`, `target.<name>` | Passes of your own. See [Passes & inputs](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/shaderpacks/passes-and-inputs.md). |
| `pipeline.<knob>` | Which passes of the renderer run, and their sizes. See [The pipeline](#the-pipeline). |

## Options

An option is a setting that the player can change on the Graphics page. Your shaders read it as a define.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `option.<id>.label`, `.tooltip` | The text that the window shows. |
| `option.<id>.default` | The default value. Required. |
| `option.<id>.values` | A choice. Its values have spaces between them. Use letters, digits, `_`, `.` and `-`. |
| `option.<id>.value.<value>` | The text that the window shows for one value of a choice. |
| `option.<id>.range` | A number: `min max step`. |
| `option.<id>.kept` | `true`: only the player sets it. No preset sets it, and a change never makes the preset **Custom**. |
| `option.<id>.disabledBy` | Another toggle or choice of the pack. While it is on, the window greys out this option and keeps its value. |

An option with no `values` and no `range` is a toggle: `true` or `false`.

**Names in GLSL.** Every shader stage gets these defines after its `#version` line:

- `OPTION_<ID>` for each option: `shadowResolution` becomes `OPTION_SHADOW_RESOLUTION`. A toggle is `1` or `0`. A
  number is its value. A choice of words is the index of the chosen word. Each word also gets a define with its index,
  for example `OPTION_SKY_FLAT 0` and `OPTION_SKY_GRADIENT 1`.
- `PIPELINE_<KNOB>` for each pipeline knob, in capitals with underscores: `PIPELINE_SHADOW_RESOLUTION 2048`.

A library file that reads an option gives it a default with `#ifndef`. A pack that does not have the option does not
define it.

**Saved values.** Each option is a live setting named `pack.<encoded id>.<option id>` in
`Zomboid/viewpoint-live.properties`. The encoded id writes `.` and `-` as `_`. For `example.dusk`, the setting for
`warmth` is `pack.example_dusk.warmth`. See [Package kinds](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/concepts/package-kinds.md#the-encoded-id).

## Presets

The **Quality** list is the first option of a pack on the Graphics page. It lists your presets, then **Custom**. When the
player chooses a preset, Viewpoint sets the options to its values. When the player changes an option away from the
preset, the list shows **Custom**.

- `preset.<id>` lists values as `option=value`, with spaces between them. An option that the line leaves out takes its
  default.
- `preset.<id>.label` is the name in the list. Without it, the id in words: `veryHigh` is "Very high".
- The preset of `preset.default` must give every option its default. Its line is usually empty. Viewpoint tells you if it
  does not, because the list would show **Custom** from the start.
- This list is not the **Preset** of the Graphics page (Potato to Ultra). That one sets the mod's own settings, never an
  option of a pack.

A line of a preset names the option or the preset that is wrong. Viewpoint leaves out a pack that has an error in
`pack.properties`. The Graphics page lists it under **Left out** with the reason.

## The pipeline

The pipeline says which passes of the renderer run for your pack, and their sizes. A knob that you leave out keeps the
value of the base. A pass that is off is not drawn. This is where a light pack saves its time.

A value can follow an option: `pipeline.shadowResolution=${shadowResolution}`.

| Knob | Library value | What it switches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `shadows` | `true` | The shadows of the sun and the moon. |
| `shadowResolution` | `2048` | The texels along one side of each shadow map, 256 to 16384. |
| `shadowCascades` | `3` | The number of shadow maps about the player: 1, 2 or 3. |
| `flashlightShadow` | `true` | The shadow of the flashlight, and of a muzzle flash. |
| `lampShadows` | `2` | How many of the nearest lamps cast shadows, 0 to 8. |
| `farShadows` | `true` | The shadows of the far world. |
| `clouds` | `true` | The volumetric clouds. |
| `cloudResolution` | `50` | The size of the clouds' image as a share of the frame, in percent, 25 to 100. |
| `volumetrics` | `true` | The light in the air: haze, god rays, halos of lamps and the beam of the flashlight. |
| `occlusion` | `true` | The occlusion of ambient light. |
| `bounce` | `true` | The light that the floors bounce. |
| `bloom` | `true` | The bloom. |
| `antialiasing` | `taaPlus` | One of `off`, `fxaa`, `smaa`, `taa`, `taaFxaa`, `taaPlus`. |
| `puddles` | `true` | Wet ground and puddles. |

The renderer has more knobs. The library file that uses a knob names it in its first lines.

## Build on another pack

`base=` names the pack that yours starts from. It can be one of these:

| Base | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `library` | The full look as the renderer draws it, with its options. The model for a pack that changes a little: replace `post.frag` for a new grade. |
| `vivid` | The full look, warmer and bolder. It holds still as Viewpoint changes. |
| `default` | The pack that the Modern mode uses until the player chooses another. It goes further than `vivid`, and it changes as Viewpoint changes. |
| The id of a folder pack | A pack that the player has in their folder. |
| The id of another package | A Shaderpack from another mod. |

If you want a look that holds still, start from `library` or `vivid`.

A pack starts with the options, presets and pipeline lines of its base. Then it adds its own.

- An option with the id of a base option replaces it, in the same place in the list.
- A `preset.<id>` line for a preset of the base adds values over the base's line.
- Pipeline lines work in the same way.

### Chaining across packages

When the base is another package, these rules apply:

- Put the base in `requires`. Without it, the pack does not start, and the card says **requires its base**.
- While the base is not active, the card shows **Waiting for \<base\>**. The pack starts when the base is active.
- A cycle of bases is refused.
- A change to a base reads its dependents again. No pack keeps an old base.
- Shaderpacks are not in an order. They never stack by their place in a list. The only stacking is `base=`.

> **Note**
>
> The pass API of Shaderpacks has a version. An addon asks for it with `Version.has("passes", generation)`. Set
> `viewpoint.min` for a Shaderpack that needs a newer Viewpoint.

## Limits

A Shaderpack that comes as a package is read one time, when Viewpoint finds the package, and Viewpoint compiles from
this copy. These limits are for such a package.

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| One file | 16 MiB |
| All files of one pack | 64 MiB |
| Files in one pack | 1,000 |
| Links | None. A link, a junction or a special file in the pack folder makes Viewpoint refuse the pack. |
| File names | No device names (`aux`, `nul`), no `:`, and no name that ends with a dot or a space |
| Text files | `pack.properties` and the files in `shaders/` must be UTF-8 |

If a pack is over a limit, Viewpoint refuses it. The card names the file.

## When something is wrong

- **In `pack.properties`:** Viewpoint leaves out the pack. The Graphics page lists it under **Left out** with the reason.
  `console.txt` has the same line.
- **In a GLSL file:** the renderer keeps the pack that it had, or the library at the start. The Graphics page shows the
  compiler's errors with file names and line numbers. `console.txt` has them also.

The files that the player accepted are the files that Viewpoint compiles.

---

# Passes & inputs

> Add full-screen passes to a Shaderpack. The stages, the inputs, the values of the frame, the event values and the values of addons.

A Shaderpack can add full-screen passes. A pass is a fragment shader of your own. Viewpoint draws it over the whole
frame at one stage. It reads what you name, and it writes the image of the stage or a target of your pack. Use a pass for
an effect that the renderer does not have: motion blur, depth of field, a lens flare, reflections.

```properties title="pack.properties"
targets=focus
target.focus=r16f 1x1 history

passes=focus dof
pass.focus.stage=final
pass.focus.fragment=focus.frag
pass.focus.inputs=depth focus.previous
pass.focus.target=focus

pass.dof.stage=final
pass.dof.fragment=dof.frag
pass.dof.inputs=color depth focus
pass.dof.when=depthOfField
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `passes` | The ids of your passes. Within a stage they run in this order. |
| `pass.<id>.stage` | `translucent`, `composite` or `final`. Required. |
| `pass.<id>.fragment` | Its fragment shader: a path in `shaders/`. Required. |
| `pass.<id>.vertex` | Its vertex shader. The default is `screen.vert`: one triangle over the screen, with `vUv` from 0 to 1. |
| `pass.<id>.inputs` | What it reads, with spaces between the names. Use at most 12. |
| `pass.<id>.target` | What it writes: `color` (the image of the stage, the default) or one of your targets. |
| `pass.<id>.when` | A toggle option of your pack. The pass runs only while it is on. |
| `targets` | The names of your targets. Use at most 8. |
| `target.<name>` | `<format> <size> [history]`. |

**Format** is `rgba8`, `rgba16f`, `rg16f`, `r16f` or `r32f`.

**Size** is a share of the frame (`1`, `0.5`, `0.25`; up to 1) or a number of texels (`1x1`, `256x256`; up to 4096).

**`history`** keeps the copy of the target from the end of the last frame.

## The stages

| Stage | When it runs | What `color` is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `translucent` | After the glass. Before the bounce light, the weather and the air. | The lit HDR image, with the depth of the scene drawn. |
| `composite` | After the air and the bloom. Before `post.frag`. | The HDR image that `post.frag` is about to read. |
| `final` | After anti-aliasing. Before the rain over the image. | The finished image, after the tone curve. |

- What a pass writes at `translucent` or `composite` goes into the history of anti-aliasing. This is what reflections
  want, because anti-aliasing smooths their noise.
- The history of anti-aliasing is taken before `final`. A blur at `final` never smears into the next frames.
- At `final`, the image can be at the size of the screen while the other inputs are at the size of the frame. Read the
  other inputs by their UV.
- Without a pass at `final`, the frame is drawn as without passes. A pack with no passes pays nothing.

## The inputs

An input goes on a sampler. Its name is `u` and the input name with a capital letter: `color` is `uColor`, `farDepth` is
`uFarDepth`, `focus.previous` is `uFocusPrevious`.

| Input | Holds | At which stages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `color` | The image of the stage, as the previous pass left it. | All |
| `depth` | The depth of the scene. `lib/camera.glsl` turns it into a position. | All |
| `albedo`, `normal`, `light` | The G-buffer: colour and material, normal, and the light of the game's grids. | All |
| `velocity` | How far the models moved on screen since the last frame, in UV. `w` is 1 where it is set. | All |
| `farDepth` | The depth of the far world, on its own range (`uFarRange`). Set only where the far world drew. | All |
| `occlusion` | The ambient occlusion: the bent normal and the visibility. | All |
| `volume` | The light in the air, at half size. | `composite`, `final` |
| `bloom` | The first level of the bloom. The bloom of the pack must be on. | `composite`, `final` |
| `<target>` | A target of your pack: what a pass before this pass wrote in this frame. | All |
| `<target>.previous` | A target with `history`: what it held at the end of the last frame. Zeros in the first frame. | All |

A pass cannot read the target that it writes. Read `<target>.previous` for the last frame.

> **Note**
>
> Each pass is one full-screen draw. Your targets use video memory. Viewpoint makes them when your pack comes into use,
> and lets them go when another pack comes into use. A pass that does not compile does not replace the pack on screen.
> The Graphics page shows the errors.

## The values of the frame

Viewpoint sets these uniforms once each frame, on every pass that declares them. Declare only the ones that you use.

| Uniform | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `uResolution`, `uTexel` (`vec2`) | The size of what the pass writes, and one over it. |
| `uView`, `uProjection` (`mat4`) | The camera's view and projection. |
| `uViewProjection`, `uInvViewProjection` (`mat4`) | From scene space to clip space and back. |
| `uPrevious` (`mat4`) | From this frame's scene position to the clip position of the last frame. |
| `uCamera` (`vec4`), `uEye` (`vec3`) | The near and far planes and the tangents of the half-angles. The eye in scene space. |
| `uSunDir`, `uSunColor` (`vec3`), `uSunStrength` (`float`) | The direction, colour and strength of the sun, or of the moon at night. |
| `uFogColor` (`vec3`), `uFogRange` (`vec2`) | The colour of the fog, and where it starts and ends, in squares. |
| `uTime`, `uFrameSeconds`, `uExposure` (`float`), `uFrame` (`int`) | Real seconds. How long the last frame took. The exposure. The number of frames drawn. |
| `uRain`, `uSnow` (`float`) | How hard it rains and snows, 0 to 1. |
| `uWind` (`vec2`) | The wind at the ground, in squares each second. |
| `uCloudCover` (`float`) | How much of the sky over the eye is cloud, 0 to 1. |
| `uSceneOrigin` (`vec3`) | Where the origin of the scene is in the world. |

Scene space has x to the west, y up and z to the north, relative to the character. One storey is the side of a square
multiplied by √6.

> **Fix things to the world**
>
> Anything that is fixed to the world needs `uSceneOrigin` added back. Without it, patterns crawl and shadows slide when the
> player walks.

Do not use `uTime` for the weather. The weather follows the game's clock, so a paused game stills the clouds. Use the
values of the weather that `lib/weather.glsl` declares.

## Event values

Viewpoint sets a value for each event of the fight: a muzzle flash, a shot, a hit on a zombie, and damage that the player
takes. The names start with `uEvent`. Each value tells how long ago the last event happened, and how strong it was.
Declare the uniform to read it.

| Uniform | Event |
| --- | --- |
| `uniform vec2 uEventFlash;` | A muzzle flash: 1 for your own gun, less for a gun further away, 0 at 30 squares or more |
| `uniform vec2 uEventShot;` | A shot that you fire |
| `uniform vec2 uEventHit;` | A zombie that you hit: 1, or 0.5 for a blow that does no damage |
| `uniform vec2 uEventDamage;` | Damage that you take: 1 for a quarter of your health or more |

`x` is the seconds since the last event, and `y` is its strength, from 0 to 1. Before the first event, `x` is 1000000.

Use these values for an effect that you tie to the fight, for example a short vignette. Do not use them to copy a cue
that the game does not give.

## Values of addons

An addon can give a value to your shaders. See [Shader values](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/api/shader-values.md). Declare the uniform with the
encoded id of the addon in its name:

```glsl
uniform float uAddon_example_lean_angle;
```

For the addon `example.lean` and the value `angle`, the name is `uAddon_example_lean_angle`. The name of a value has no
`_` in it, so the name has one reading. If the addon is off,
Viewpoint does not set the uniform. Make your shader work with a value of 0. Add the addon to `requires` if your pack is
not useful without it.

---

# Library files

> Replace files of Viewpoint's shader library by path, keep the snippet markers, and follow the rules of the files that need care.

Viewpoint draws the world with a library of GLSL files. A Shaderpack changes the look by replacing some of them.

## Replace a file

A file in the `shaders/` folder of your pack replaces the file of the same path in the library.

- The library is in Viewpoint's source repository, in `src/main/resources/viewpoint/shaders/`.
- Files in `lib/` can also be replaced. Each program that includes the file gets your version.
- A file that you do not replace comes from your `base`, then from the library. A pack holds only what it changes.
- `constants.glsl` cannot be replaced. Viewpoint makes it. Any file can `#include "constants.glsl"`.
- Every stage starts with `#version 330`. Viewpoint adds the defines of the options and the pipeline after this line.
  See [Format](https://docs.projectviewpoint.org/shaderpacks/format.md#options).

An include is a line of this form. Viewpoint expands it before it compiles the file, and it adds `#line` directives so
that an error names the file and the line.

```glsl
#include "lib/sun.glsl"
```

An include path is relative to the `shaders/` folder. Viewpoint reads `./` and `//` in it as plain. It refuses a file
whose include path holds `..`, an absolute path or `\`.

> **Tip**
>
> Read the library file that you replace first. Its first lines say what it does and which uniforms it gets. Your file can
> leave out the uniforms that it does not use.

## Files that are easy to replace

A shared file in `lib/` is the cheapest file to replace. One change then applies to the near world and the far world.

| File | Controls |
| --- | --- |
| `lib/shade.glsl` | The lighting model. The deferred, forward and far passes all call it. |
| `lib/fog.glsl` | The colour of the fog: what the world fades into at the end of the fog. |
| `lib/fog_amount.glsl` | How much fog a point gets. Keep the end of the fog where the range puts it: past it nothing is drawn. |
| `lib/distance.glsl` | What the distance does to a colour. |
| `lib/sun_filter.glsl` | The filter of the sun's shadows. |
| `lib/cloud_shadow.glsl` | The shadow of the clouds on the sun's light. |
| `lib/precip_look.glsl` | The look of rain, snow and splashes. |
| `post.frag` | The composite: the fog, the tone curve and the grade. |
| `sky.frag` | The sky. |

The weather is Viewpoint's. How it looks is the pack's. Two files are always the library's, and a copy in your pack is
not used: `lib/weather.glsl` and `precip.vert`. The console names the copy when the pack loads.

## Rules for some files

Some files must follow a rule, or the picture breaks.

- **Models of packs.** A replaced `mesh.vert` or `shadow.vert` must include `lib/pack_model.glsl`. While `uModels` is
  set, it must take its vertex from `modelVertex(aPos, aUv, aNormal)`, as the library files do. A program without
  `uModels` draws no models of packs.
- **Dead bodies.** A replaced `mesh.vert` or `shadow.vert` must include `lib/corpse_card.glsl`. While `uCards` is set, it
  must take its vertex from `cardVertex()`.
- **Characters and items.** A replaced `model_gbuffer.frag`, `model_shadow.frag` or `model_outline.frag` reads
  `uTextures[vTexture]`, not `uTexture`. It needs `#extension GL_ARB_gpu_shader5 : enable`.
- **The far shell.** A replaced `far_shell.frag`, `gbuffer_shell.frag` or `far_shadow_shell.frag` reads
  `uAtlases[vAtlas]`.
- **Glass.** Keep the rule of the library in `gbuffer.frag` and `forward.frag`. Glass for which `glassSolid` is true is
  solid in the G-buffer. It is not in the translucent pass. Otherwise a window shows the empty rooms behind it.
- **Translucent texels.** A replaced `forward.frag` or `vehicle_glass.frag` writes each texel through
  `translucent(colour, alpha, fromEye)`. Do not declare an output of your own.
- **The sun's light.** The direct light of the sun must fall to none as `uSunStrength` falls, at dusk and at dawn. Follow
  `uSunStrength`, as the library does. Otherwise the light drops in one frame.
- **Includes of options.** A library file that reads an option gives it a default with `#ifndef`.

## The markers for snippets

Addons can add snippets of GLSL to your shaders. Most points work with any file. They are the start and the end of a
